voiceover: Every movement leads with its best foot. The earliest Christians led with their worst. At the center of their message was not a teaching or a miracle, but an execution: a man Rome had nailed to a cross, the death it reserved for slaves and rebels. Crucifixion was what Josephus called the most wretched of deaths, so degrading that polite Romans avoided the word. For a first-century Jew it was worse. The Law said: a hanged man is cursed by God. So a crucified Messiah was very nearly a contradiction in terms. Paul knew it exactly: we preach Christ crucified, a stumbling block to Jews and folly to Gentiles. The crucifixion is, by wide agreement, the most secure single fact about Jesus. Its bedrock status rests first on plain attestation: it is reported even by the Roman historian Tacitus, and by Josephus. The scandal adds a second, converging consideration: inventors do not sabotage their own inventions. And the first Christians did not hide it. They gloried in it: far be it from me to boast except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ. Paul's answer runs straight through the offending text: Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us. The scandal is not denied; it is absorbed and turned inside out. The first Christians staked everything on it, and we say it with them: the crucified Jesus is the Messiah, and God raised him.
